narrative:
The model estimated a 71% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is a high-risk prediction, and it is why your law-school application was denied: the decision treated your likely bar outcome as too risky to admit you.

The strongest influence was your LSAT score of 25, which is well below the average of about 37 among accepted students; this pushed the prediction toward failure. The second strongest was your third-year class standing (decile 3, compared with an accepted-student average of about 5.8), which also pushed toward failure. The third was your first-year class standing (decile 5, compared with an average of about 6); although it was below the accepted average, it was the one top factor that leaned toward passing rather than failing. Overall, the LSAT and third-year standing outweighed that positive signal, producing the denial.

To improve your position, ask admissions for feedback and speak with a pre-law advisor. If possible, retake the LSAT after focused preparation, address any explainable academic difficulties, and show measurable improvement through additional coursework or a strengthened record before reapplying. You may also ask whether a written explanation or addendum can accompany a future application. Reapplication is more likely to be competitive once the strongest failure signals—especially the LSAT and later academic standing—have improved.
